newNecessary.meaningAndRegister: An imperial edict/order, encountered in historical and governmental writing. Daijisen sense1 includes sovereigns/kings; sense2 is the particular Meiji-Constitution legal form. Give the Japanese historical legal setting as one use, not the only geographic/historical use, and not a claim about the present validity of every old edict.

newNecessary.comparison: Link existing命令めいれい as the broader order/command noun; a supervisor's everyday order is not normally called勅令. No fixed opposite is established. Do not equate any order with an imperial edict or classify all historical legal instruments as identical.
guardRationale: 命令 displays order;command; its full1532160 also has decree/directive. A broader command label is defensible for an imperial edict.

命じる/命ずる display bare order/command before appoint. Their complete verbal families support the instruction meaning; these conservative quiz guards avoid the unmarked English noun/verb ambiguity. They do not assert identical Japanese parts of speech or appointment senses.

法/法律/規則 have broad law/regulation labels. A legal edict can be understood as law/regulation; these conservative direct quiz guards prevent that broad-label ambiguity without equating every law, method or school rule with an imperial edict.
